title: Close Enough: Choosing a Tolerance That Means Something

questions.question: You compare two doubles with an absolute tolerance of 1e-9. Roughly how many distinct representable doubles does that tolerance cover at magnitude 1, and at magnitude 1e9?
options: The same number at both: a tolerance is a tolerance
About a thousand at magnitude 1, and about a million at 1e9
One at magnitude 1, and about 4.5 million at 1e9
About 4.5 million at magnitude 1, and less than one at 1e9
questions.explanation: Doubles are not spread evenly. The gap between neighbours is 2.2e-16 near 1 and 1.2e-7 near 1e9, so a fixed distance means two completely different things. Both ends are wrong: loose at the bottom, unsatisfiable at the top.

questions.question: At magnitude 1e9 the gap between neighbouring doubles is 1.19e-7. What does a tolerance of 1e-9 mean there?
options: No two distinct doubles can satisfy it, so a loop waiting for agreement can only stop on an identical bit pattern
It rounds up to the gap, so it behaves as 1.19e-7
It is very strict but achievable with enough iterations
It is undefined behaviour
questions.explanation: There is nothing between a value and its neighbour. A tolerance smaller than that gap is not strict, it is impossible, and that is the difference between a slow algorithm and one that cannot terminate.

questions.question: Why does nearly_equal need an absolute tolerance as well as a relative one?
options: To make it faster, by skipping the multiply in the common case
To handle infinity and NaN
Near zero there is no magnitude to be relative to, so 1e-18 and 2e-18 come out a hundred percent apart
Because relative tolerances do not work on negative numbers
questions.explanation: Relative alone cannot reach zero and absolute alone cannot reach 1e9, so the comparison passes if either does. The absolute one is a floor for the neighbourhood of zero and is there for nothing else.

questions.question: A loop does t += 0.1 and stops when t < 10.0 becomes false. How many steps does it take?
options: It never stops
99, because the accumulated value overshoots
100, exactly as arithmetic says
101, because a hundred additions of 0.1 reach 9.99999999999998046
questions.explanation: The accumulated clock lands just under ten, so the condition is still true and the loop takes one more step. Writing t != 10.0 instead never terminates at all. Deriving t from an integer step index and multiplying is exact: 100 * 0.1 is exactly 10.0.

questions.question: You add 1.0 to a running total of 1e16, a hundred thousand times. How much does the total change?
options: By 100000, as expected
Not at all: the gap between doubles at 1e16 is 2.0, so every addition is discarded
By about 50000, since half the additions round up
By 100000 but with accumulated rounding error of a few units
questions.explanation: The sum comes out bit for bit equal to 1e16, an error of exactly -100000. Not rounded, discarded. Sorting smallest first gives the exact answer, and so does kahan_sum without reordering anything.

questions.question: In kahan_sum, why must (next - total) - adjusted keep its parentheses?
options: Algebraically it is zero, and in floating point it is the part that did not fit, so reassociating it throws the correction away
To avoid integer overflow in the intermediate
Because subtraction is not commutative
For readability only
questions.explanation: Floating point addition is not associative, which is both why the algorithm is needed and how it works. An optimiser permitted to reassociate the expression, which -ffast-math permits, computes zero and silently reduces the function to plain addition.
